newsitem.title: USA: AMR strike could hurt U.S. airline industry.
newsitem.headline: AMR strike could hurt U.S. airline industry.

text.p: Labor strife at AMR Corp's American Airlines threatens to open a breach between management and labor that could slam the brakes on the profit growth of U.S. carriers, analysts said.

Pilots at American Airlines could strike February 15 if last-ditch negotiations with management next week failed to produce a settlement. Many analysts believe the effects of a strike would ripple throughout the industry.

Labor groups at rival carriers would gain strength from a strike at American, analysts said. A job action by the pilots, who seek paybacks for wage concessions made during the industry's downturn, would intensify efforts by employees of other carriers to grab a bigger share of airlines' record profits.

"An American strike would mean an extreme rupture of trust across the industry," said Joseph Blasi, a professor at Rutgers University's School of Management and Labor Relations. "It would remind many airline workers how angry they are ... and would harden positions at other airlines," Blasi said.

"It's an industry that tends to look at other carriers as a benchmark. Continental and USAir seem to be the most at risk," said SBC Warburg Inc analyst Timothy Ross. A possible strike at American "gives them another lever to use in talks," Ross said.
Continental Airlines Inc will begin wage negotiations with its pilots in April. UAL Corp's pilots recently rejected a midterm wage agreement and must submit to binding arbitration.

Meanwhile, USAir Group Inc has presented a "wish list" to its pilots that calls for pay cuts of about 12 percent at a time when workers at other airlines are seeking double-digit pay increases, sources said.

Even if the airlines reach labor settlements, tension will with unions will remain, analysts said. Disgruntled workers can hurt an airline in subtle ways, such as on-time performance, customer service and baggage handling -- which could slowly erode profits, analysts said.

Both the pilots and American management have said they want a negotiated settlement to the bitter dispute, but remain far apart on some major issues. Final talks begin February 10 and will center on issues such as stock options and wage increases. The pilots also demanded that American not use its American Eagle commuter airline, which employs pilots of another union, to fly 50-passenger regional jets.

SBC Warburg's Ross estimated a strike would cost AMR $23 million a day in earnings, or $0.25 a share. The airline could handle 42 days of strike before hitting negative earnings territory, he said. Other analysts said the daily costs would be even higher.
Some analysts suggested that if AMR met the pilots' demands, management could trim operations and eventually sell the airline.

American said a 60-day pilot strike would hurt the U.S. economy by about $4.75 billion, including direct and indirect employment costs, lost tax revenue and negative impact on suppliers and the tourism industry.
American, however, declined to comment on how much it would lose during a possible strike.

But the airline has already started feeling the effects of a strike. Advanced bookings have fallen off as passengers shift to other carriers to avoid being stranded, analysts said. To win back passengers, American would have to slash fares -- perhaps sparking fare war throughout the industry.
"Even if a strike is avoided, there is damage being done," said Salomon Brothers analyst Julius Maldutis.
